entities.name: Delhi Sultanate
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526 CE), founded by Qutb ud-Din Aibak — a Turkic slave general of the Ghurid rulers of Afghanistan — was the first major Islamic empire in South Asia, ruling the Indian subcontinent for 320 years through five successive Turkic and Afghan dynasties. The Sultanate repelled the Mongol invasions of the 13th century (when the Mongols destroyed every major civilization from Baghdad to Korea), preserving Islamic civilization in South Asia while Baghdad, Merv, and Samarkand burned. The Qutb Minar (1193-1220) in Delhi remains the world's tallest brick minaret.

Qutb ud-Din Aibak, a slave (mamluk) soldier who rose to become governor of northern India under Muhammad of Ghor, declared independence after his master's assassination in 1206 — founding the 'Slave Dynasty,' the first of five Delhi Sultanate dynasties. The Sultanate's most significant act was Iltutmish's successful resistance of the Mongol armies of Genghis Khan's grandsons — turning them back at the Indus River three times (1221, 1228, 1241), sparing Delhi while the Mongols destroyed Baghdad (1258) and burned Central Asia's libraries and cities.

The Delhi Sultanate brought Persian as the court language, Islamic law (sharia) courts, Afghan-Mughal architectural traditions, and Sufi orders to South Asia. Alauddin Khalji's market reforms (1303-1316) — fixing prices of grain, cloth, and cattle — represent medieval India's most ambitious economic intervention. The Sultanate was finally destroyed by Babur's Mughal invasion at the First Battle of Panipat (1526), which substituted Mughal for Afghan-Turkic rule.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Delhi Sultanate's three repulsions of the Mongol invasions that destroyed Baghdad and Central Asia — preserving Islamic South Asian civilization during the 13th century's greatest catastrophe — was the most consequential military achievement in South Asian history.
